title: Who is left standing?
hook: One candidate, one counter, seven items. Which item survives the cancelling?

doesNotKnow: that one candidate and one counter find an item filling more than half a stream, and only that: with no such item the survivor means nothing until a second pass checks it

misconception: The item left standing after cancelling pairs of different items is the most common one.
objective: The learner can explain that each -1 cancels two different items, so an item filling more than half the stream (A, 5 of 7 in stream 2) must survive, but with no such item the survivor can be anything (C, only 2 of 7 in stream 1, while A had 3), so a second pass must check it.

claims.text: With the rule (same item as the candidate +1, different -1, at 0 the next item becomes the candidate), stream 1, A A A B B C C, ends with candidate C (counter 1), and stream 2, A A B A C A A, ends with candidate A (counter 3).
claims.source: run() in src/demos/cs/last-survivor-is-not-the-most-common/model.ts. Builder's node run 2026-10-14: stream 1 counters A1 A2 A3 A2 A1 A0 C1; stream 2 A1 A2 A1 A2 A1 A2 A3. The fact-checker can redo both by hand (7 steps each).

claims.text: In stream 1, A appears 3 times and C 2 times, and no item fills more than half the stream (which needs 4 of 7); in stream 2, A fills 5 of 7.
claims.source: Counting the tiles: stream 1 A 3, B 2, C 2; stream 2 A 5, B 1, C 1.

claims.text: Each -1 cancels two different items, so if an item fills more than half the stream, that many copies cannot all be cancelled and it is the final candidate.
claims.source: Each decrement pairs one copy of the candidate with one different item and removes both from consideration; a majority item has more copies than all other items together, so it cannot be fully paired off (Boyer and Moore's correctness argument).

claims.text: With no item in more than half the stream, the survivor proves nothing, so a second pass is needed to check that the candidate really is a majority.
claims.source: Stream 1 is a counterexample: the survivor C is not the most common item (A, 3 vs 2) and not a majority. Counting the candidate in a second pass decides whether a majority exists.

claims.text: One counter finds a majority if there is one (the Boyer-Moore majority vote method).
claims.source: Boyer and Moore (1991), 'MJRTY: A Fast Majority Vote Algorithm', in Automated Reasoning: Essays in Honor of Woody Bledsoe (Kluwer), 105-117. The lesson does not name the method on the learner's screen; the name is recorded here for the fact-checker. Attribution: fact-checker confirms.

recall.question: You run the one-candidate, one-counter method over a list of votes and it ends with candidate Q. What do you know about Q before counting again?
options: Q is the most common vote
If any vote is a majority, it is Q
Q got more than half the votes
recall.why: A majority item cannot be cancelled away, so it must survive; but with no majority the survivor can be anything. A second pass counts Q to check.
